title: HTTP 402: Teaching the Web to Let Agents Pay

back with some recommendations. And he's doing great, but by the time it goes into the third website, it hits a wall. And you know,

And so, here's the strange and interesting part because the web saw this coming about 30 years ago. Because in the HTTP spec, right next to the 404

All right. And then if we look at option three, say we charge a flat subscription, um that also breaks because the agents they don't consume

And I would say that's why you see industries moving more and more towards that metered usage-based billing. And And it's because the natural unit of

and then we're going to come back to that question about guarantees. So, the standard relies on five different pieces. You first have the client, so that's your agent that holds
the wallet, a way to move value and it can sign. Then you also have the resource server, that's the thing with the API or the content that you want and
the thing behind the paywall. You also have a facilitator and that's probably the piece that most of us haven't heard of and that's a service
that actually checks and settles the payment so that the resource server actually doesn't have to talk to a blockchain. And then you have the settlement layer,
uh so that's a distributed ledger like Hedera, Ethereum, and others. And of course, the stable coin, which is going to be the unit of account here, so
something like digital dollars or USDC. And then I would say in the simplest terms, you can think about this X402 as three very simple steps. You have the request, you
have one rejection with like a menu, and then you have a retry with a payment authorization. So, if we look at this more detailed sequence view, what you have is
it all starts with the agent making that normal request. So, for example, get premium data. So, it just asks for that. The server says, "No, I actually need a payment for
this." And it embeds in that response a machine-readable uh menu with information about what how much to pay, the token, the network, and to which
address. The agent then reads that menu, and then it picks an option, you know, signs the payment authorization. That's a signature that happens off-chain, so
hasn't touched the blockchain. And then, the you know, the agent sends that back to the server, but this time with a signature attached to that in a header
called payment signature. Now, the server is going to hand that to the facilitator to ask two things. First, is this valid? That's the verify call, and then once
that's verified, the server uh does the work. Then, uh the settle call happens, and the facilitator pushes that on the chain and pays the gas fee, the transaction cost
on the chain. And then finally, you have the transaction is confirmed, the server gets the the the transaction confirmation, it serves your data, also
with a 200 status code, and it includes the receipt for proving the payment. And so, what you see here is that the entire process is just HTTP and on
off-chain signature, and the blockchain is just touched once in that purple arrow at the end. So, you know, that's how that agent that was stuck behind the paywall can
actually pay a few cents or a few dollars and get the answer it was looking for. Now, I do want to zoom into a couple of aspects here in this diagram

You also want deterministic finality. So, the agent and the server, they have to know, they have to be sure that the money is truly
